::: {.oneline}
The self-energy is everything the rest of the system does to a particle passing
through it: it shifts the particle's energy, gives it a finite lifetime, and
makes it less like the particle you started with.
:::

## Short answer

A ball bearing falling through honey does not behave like a ball bearing falling
through air. It responds as though it were heavier (it has to drag the fluid
along) and it slows down, since it loses energy to the fluid. Neither effect is
a property of the ball or of the honey taken separately.

An electron moving through a solid is in the same situation. It repels the other
electrons, so that a region of reduced density travels with it, and this cloud
has to be carried along. The self-energy is the name we give to the whole
influence: it is what we must add to the free particle energy in order to
describe the composite object that actually propagates.

We can therefore expect three effects at once. The energy is shifted (this is
why a computed band gap moves once interactions are included), the lifetime
becomes finite, since the added particle can share its energy with other
excitations and stop being recognizable, and part of the weight is removed from
the particle-like feature of the spectrum and redistributed into a broad
background carrying no sharp energy at all.

When the shift is moderate and the lifetime long, the composite object is a
quasiparticle, and the familiar single-particle language survives with renamed
parameters. When the lifetime is short there is no particle left to speak of.
This is not a failure of the calculation, but the physics itself.

## Why it works this way

The self-energy exists because the separation between "the particle" and "the
medium" is a choice and not a fact. The choice is nevertheless a useful one,
since it allows us to retain a single-particle vocabulary, and the self-energy
is the exact price we pay for it, collecting everything that the separation has
left out.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: Dyson's equation

The dressed propagator is built from the bare one by repeated insertion of the
self-energy $\Sigma$:

$$
G = G_0 + G_0\,\Sigma\,G ,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
G^{-1} = G_0^{-1} - \Sigma .
$$ {#eq-dyson}

Near a quasiparticle pole, $\operatorname{Re}\Sigma$ shifts the energy,
$\operatorname{Im}\Sigma$ sets the inverse lifetime, and the derivative of
$\operatorname{Re}\Sigma$ with respect to frequency gives the quasiparticle
weight

$$
Z = \left(1 - \frac{\partial \operatorname{Re}\Sigma}{\partial\omega}\right)^{-1}
\le 1 ,
$$ {#eq-quasiparticle-weight}

the fraction of spectral weight still behaving like a single particle. The rest
is incoherent background.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: the GW approximation

Approximating $\Sigma$ as the product of the propagator and the screened
interaction,

$$
\Sigma(1,2) = i\, G(1,2)\, W(1^{+},2) ,
$$ {#eq-gw}

is the standard first step for real materials. Screening is essential: using the
bare Coulomb interaction instead badly overestimates the gap, because it ignores
the fact that the other electrons move out of the way.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The self-energy is a correction, so it must be small."** In correlated
  systems it can dominate, and destroy the quasiparticle entirely.
- **"Its imaginary part is a numerical broadening parameter."** It is a physical
  decay rate. The artificial broadening we add when plotting a spectrum is a
  different quantity altogether.
